# 23 Object Storage Part 1

Part of [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/Backend from First Principles|Backend from First Principles]] · Previous: [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/22 Concurrency and Parallelism/22 Concurrency and Parallelism|22 Concurrency and Parallelism]] · Next: [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/24 Object Storage Part 2/24 Object Storage Part 2|24 Object Storage Part 2]]

Sooner or later, almost every backend has to accept **files** from users: profile pictures, documents, videos. Files look simple, but they behave very differently from the JSON data a backend usually handles. They are large, they grow forever, and they need their own kind of storage. This lesson starts with the naive approach (save the file on the server's disk), shows exactly how it breaks in production, and then builds up **object storage** (Amazon S3 and similar services): what it is, why its interface is so limited, how it works inside, and the production pattern for uploads, **pre-signed URLs**.

Part 2 continues with large files (multipart and resumable uploads), downloads, range requests and costs.

---

## 1. A new requirement: users upload files

Imagine a working backend with authentication, a database, handlers, services and repositories (everything from the earlier lessons). A new requirement arrives: **users must be able to upload a profile picture**.

The intuitive (naive) implementation:

1. The browser sends the file as **form data** (`multipart/form-data`, the encoding browsers use to send files).
2. The server pulls the file out of the request.
3. It saves the file on its **local file system**, the disk of the machine it runs on (on Linux, something like **ext4** or **XFS**).
4. It records the file's **path** in the database, so it can find the file later.
5. When the user's profile is requested, the server reads the file from that path and sends it back, and the browser shows the picture.

For small profile pictures (roughly 300 KB to 10 MB from a phone, maybe 15–20 MB from a mirrorless camera) this seems to work. Everything fits in memory and nothing spikes. But this design is wrong, and the rest of the lesson shows why.

---

## 2. Where the naive approach breaks: a 4 GB video

Next, the product needs **videos**: posts in a social feed, or videos sent in messages. Videos range from a few megabytes to **several gigabytes**. Reusing the same pattern:

- A user uploads a **4 GB** video.
- The server instance has **4 GB of memory** in total.
- The web framework "helpfully" reads the **entire file into memory** before handing it to your handler.
- The server runs **out of memory**, and the container is **killed** instantly.
- The orchestration platform restarts the container automatically, and **every file ever saved on that instance's disk is gone**: profile pictures, videos, everything.

On top of that, the backend was scaled to **three instances** last month. The files saved on the other two instances survived, but only there. A request routed to the wrong instance can't find the file, so roughly **one in three** profile-picture requests returns **404 Not Found**.

### The wrong assumption

The root mistake: treating a file as something **the application owns**. Files are a completely different **shape of data** from the JSON a server handles most of the time. They have a different **access pattern**, a different **cost profile**, and they need a different **kind of storage system**: **object storage**.

---

## 3. Problem 1: the server's disk is ephemeral

**Ephemeral** means temporary: it lasts only until the next restart.

- Most backends today run in **containers** (Docker, Kubernetes), on platforms like Railway or Render, or as serverless functions (Vercel, Netlify).
- A container's file system exists only as long as **that container** exists. A restart boots a **new container** from the same **image**. The image is the same, but the container instance and its files are brand new.
- Every **deployment** (e.g. via CI/CD) builds a new image with the latest code, destroys the old container and starts a new one. The image contains your code, **not your users' files**, so every deploy wipes any uploads stored inside the container.

This is part of why containers are called **stateless**.

**Partial fix: a persistent volume.** A **persistent volume** is storage attached to a container that survives restarts (Docker and Kubernetes are covered in [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/30 DevOps for Backend Engineers/30 DevOps for Backend Engineers|lesson 30]]). It solves the ephemeral-disk problem, but it still fails on problems 2 and 3 below.

---

## 4. Problem 2: horizontal scaling

Say there are three server instances behind a **load balancer** (see [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/21.2 Scaling and Performance Engineering Part 2/21.2 Scaling and Performance Engineering Part 2#2. Load balancers|lesson 21.2]]):

1. A user uploads a file. The load balancer routes the request to **instance 1**, which saves the file on its own disk.
2. Two minutes later, the user's browser requests the file to display it.
3. The load balancer uses **round robin** (rotate through the instances in order), so this request lands on **instance 3**.
4. Instance 3 has never heard of the file, so it returns **404**.

With *N* instances, the chance of hitting the right one is roughly **1/N**. The more you scale out, the worse it gets.

Storing files on an instance's local disk breaks the most important property of a horizontally scalable server: **statelessness**. A server should never hold state that the other servers don't have (see [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/21.2 Scaling and Performance Engineering Part 2/21.2 Scaling and Performance Engineering Part 2#1. Statelessness: the key to horizontal scaling|lesson 21.2]]).

---

## 5. Problem 3: disks have a fixed size

- You can add more **server instances** as traffic grows (horizontal scaling), but a disk can only grow by being made **bigger** (vertical scaling).
- Resizing a disk usually means detaching it, growing it and reattaching it, often with **downtime**.
- Every cloud provider has a **maximum disk size**, so there's always a ceiling.

Meanwhile, uploaded files are usually the **fastest-growing data** in an application. For example, 1,000 users uploading 100 MB each per month means **100 GB of growth every month, forever**. It rarely shrinks, because people delete files far less often than they upload them.

---

## 6. Problem 4: durability

Your server has **one disk**, and disks fail: hardware faults, power problems, crashes. Even laptop disks die. If that disk held all your users' files and was the only copy, those files are **gone**.

Two terms are worth separating:

| Term | Question it answers | Recovering from a failure |
|---|---|---|
| **Availability** | Can I reach the data **right now**? | You can **wait**: when the outage is fixed, the data is back. |
| **Durability** | Does the data **still exist** anywhere? | You **can't** wait it out. Lost data is gone forever. |

The only real answer to durability is **replication**: keeping **multiple copies** in different places. Doing it properly also requires **checksums** (to detect corrupted data) and **background repair processes** that find and fix damaged copies. That is a large, hard engineering field, not something to build yourself for a to-do app.

---

## 7. Problem 5: serving downloads

Uploads aren't the only cost. Every time someone views a file, **your server sends it**.

Example: a **50 MB** file and a user on a mobile connection of about **2 megabits per second** (megabits, not megabytes). The download takes about **3.5 minutes** (50 MB = 400 megabits; 400 ÷ 2 = 200 s).

For those minutes, one of your server's workers (a goroutine in Go, a connection in Node's event loop, a thread elsewhere) does nothing but slowly copy bytes to a distant phone. It ties up a connection, memory and bandwidth for a long time.

Your server becomes a **very expensive, very slow CDN** with a limited number of concurrent connections. **CDNs** (content delivery networks) exist precisely to do this job (see [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/21.2 Scaling and Performance Engineering Part 2/21.2 Scaling and Performance Engineering Part 2#8. CDNs: caching at a global level|lesson 21.2]]). This is I/O-bound work (see [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/22 Concurrency and Parallelism/22 Concurrency and Parallelism#2. I/O-bound vs CPU-bound|lesson 22]]) that your application servers shouldn't be doing at all if something else can.

---

## 8. Problem 6: no transaction across files and database rows

The file lives on disk and its path lives in the database: **two separate systems with no shared transaction**. A **transaction** guarantees that a group of operations either all succeed or all fail. There's nothing like that across a disk and a database.

| Order of operations | If the second step fails… | Result |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Write file → 2. Insert DB row | The row insert fails | An **orphan file**: on disk, but nothing points to it. Users can't reach it, and it costs storage money. |
| 1. Insert DB row → 2. Write file | The file write fails | A **dangling row**: the DB points to a path that doesn't exist. Every request for the picture errors (500 or 404). |

Object storage **doesn't remove** this problem, but it makes it easier to solve with a pattern, the two-phase flow in section 22.

---

## 9. Three kinds of storage

To see why object storage exists, step one level down: what kinds of storage are there? Mainly **three**, each with trade-offs.

### Block storage

- Provides a raw array of **fixed-size blocks** (typically **512 bytes** or **4 KB**), each identified by a **number**.
- The entire interface is "read block N" and "write block N", for example block 9,000,000. There are **no files, names or folders**.
- This is what a physical disk such as an **SSD** exposes, and what cloud services like **Amazon EBS** (Elastic Block Store) offer.
- **Pros:** the lowest-level and usually **fastest** option, with latency in **microseconds**. Databases like PostgreSQL and MySQL run on block storage to get that speed.
- **Cons:** the interface is far too primitive to build an application on directly. A block device is also normally attached to **one machine at a time**, so it can't be shared.

### File storage

- A **file system** (such as ext4, XFS or NTFS) is an abstraction **built on top of blocks**. It adds a **hierarchy** of directories, files, paths and permissions, tracked with internal structures such as **inodes**.
- It offers a **rich interface**: open and close files, **seek** to byte 9,000,000, **overwrite exactly four bytes** in the middle of a file, **rename** a folder instantly and **atomically**, **lock** a file, **append** to it.
- These operations are defined by **POSIX**, a standard describing what an operating system should provide. A system that implements most of it is called **POSIX-compliant**.

**The cost of convenience is coordination:**

- **Rename must be atomic**: it either fully happens or doesn't, never a half-done state. Lots of software depends on that.
- **Readers must never see half-written files.** Editors usually save by writing the new content to a **temporary file** and then **renaming** it over the original, so anyone reading gets either the old version or the new one, never a partial mix.
- **Two processes writing the same file need locking.** Log files written by several programs are the classic example.

This coordination works well on one machine but **doesn't scale** across networks, data centres and continents. **Network file systems** like **NFS** try, with their own trade-offs.

### Object storage

Object storage starts from the opposite question. Instead of *"how do we give people the richest interface?"*, it asks: *"**What is the smallest interface we can get away with**, so that it can scale without limit?"* That means **exabytes**, often called **planet scale**.

---

## 10. Object storage: the smallest possible interface

The whole interface is essentially **four operations**:

| Operation | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **PUT** | Upload an object under a name (key) |
| **GET** | Fetch an object by its name |
| **DELETE** | Delete an object by its name |
| **LIST** | List names |

### What you give up

- **No in-place changes.** You can't update, append to, seek into or partially write an object. To change one byte of a 1 GB object, you download all 1 GB, change it, and upload all 1 GB again under the same key. Objects are **immutable**: they can only be **replaced**. (That's why they're called *objects*, not *files*: "file" implies features objects don't have.)
- **No real folders.** Only **key prefixes** that imitate folders (section 12).
- **No rename.** A "rename" is a **copy to a new key plus a delete**, so it costs as much as the object's whole size.
- **No file locking** like an operating system provides.
- **Higher latency:** at least a few milliseconds, often tens, instead of microseconds, because **every operation is an HTTP request** over a network to a machine in a data centre.

### What you get in return

- **Nothing to coordinate.** With no in-place modification, a whole class of distributed-systems problems disappears.
- **No hierarchy**, so there's no directory tree to maintain, lock or rebalance.
- **Every request is self-contained HTTP**, so any of thousands of servers can handle any request. The system **scales horizontally without limit**.
- **Practically infinite capacity.** You never provision or resize anything; you just keep uploading.
- **Very high durability.** For Amazon S3, the famous **"eleven nines"** (section 16).
- **Directly addressable over HTTP.** Browsers, video players and mobile apps all speak HTTP, so they can talk to object storage **without your server in the middle**.

> [!note] A general distributed-systems pattern
> The same trade-off shows up in caching, stateless servers and immutable deployments: to reach near-unlimited scale, you usually **give up mutability** (changing things in place). Object storage is one of the purest examples.

---

## 11. What an object is

An object has four parts:

| Part | Description |
|---|---|
| **Key** | A string. It is the object's **entire identity**. |
| **Value** | The data itself: a blob of bytes (binary). |
| **System metadata** | Set by the storage service: size, last-modified time, content type, **ETag** (an identifier derived from the content, used to detect changes; HTTP ETags are covered in [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/05 HTTP for Backend Engineers/05 HTTP for Backend Engineers#9. HTTP caching|lesson 05]]). |
| **User metadata** | Your own key–value pairs, e.g. `uploaded-by: <user id>`, stored with the object. |

Objects live inside a **bucket**: a named container, one level above objects (not a folder). **Bucket names** must be **globally unique** across the whole provider (e.g. all of AWS), and each **key** is unique within its bucket, so bucket + key identifies exactly one object.

---

## 12. Folders are an illusion

In the AWS console or Cloudflare dashboard you might see a folder `uploads`, inside it `2026`, and inside that `cat.png`. That hierarchy **doesn't exist**. There is just **one object** whose key is the whole string:

```text
uploads/2026/cat.png
```

The `/` characters are ordinary characters in the key, with no special meaning to storage. There are no parent objects and no nesting: just a bucket holding a huge number of string keys.

### How the console invents folders

```bash
# Illustrative AWS CLI commands
aws s3api put-object --bucket demo-bucket --key uploads/2026/cat.png --body cat.png

aws s3api list-objects-v2 --bucket demo-bucket
# → one key: "uploads/2026/cat.png"

aws s3api list-objects-v2 --bucket demo-bucket --prefix uploads/ --delimiter /
# → "CommonPrefixes": [ { "Prefix": "uploads/2026/" } ]
```

When you list with a **prefix** (`uploads/`) and a **delimiter** (`/`), the service:

1. finds every key that starts with the prefix,
2. looks at the rest of each key, and if it contains the delimiter, **cuts it off there**,
3. reports each distinct result **once** as a **common prefix**.

That's the whole "folder feature": a **group-by on strings**.

### Consequences

- **Moving a "folder" is slow and costs money.** There's no folder to move; each of, say, 40,000 objects has to be copied to a new key and the old one deleted.
- **Empty folders can't really exist**, because a folder has no identity of its own. Some tools fake one with a **zero-byte object whose key ends in `/`**.

---

## 13. Designing object keys

Since the key is the object's whole identity, choosing its format is a real design decision.

### Rule 1 (non-negotiable): never use the user's file name as the key

1. **Collisions.** If two users upload `resume.pdf`, the second silently replaces the first. The upload operation is **PUT**, which (as in HTTP; see [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/05 HTTP for Backend Engineers/05 HTTP for Backend Engineers#6. HTTP methods|lesson 05]]) means "**replace** whatever is at this key", with no error and no warning, unlike POST's "always create new".
2. **Path traversal.** File names can contain dots, slashes and other special characters (e.g. `../`). Depending on what you do with the name later, it could **escape the prefix** you meant to write into.
3. **Unexpected characters.** Emoji, right-to-left override characters, null bytes: anything a user sends can turn into a bug downstream.

**Instead:** **generate the key yourself** (ideally something random, like a UUID) and store the **original file name in your database** (and optionally in the object's user metadata). Use the original name only when showing or downloading the file.

### Rule 2: put the random part early in the key

The storage service **partitions its index by key prefix** (section 17). A key like `uploads/<timestamp>/<id>` means every upload in the same hour shares the same prefix, so all writes hit **the same index partition**: a **hot partition**. Under heavy traffic this shows up as **503 Slow Down** errors.

The fix is to put something with high **entropy** (highly random and well spread out) near the start: a UUID, a user or tenant ID, or the first few characters of a hash.

```text
✗ uploads/2026-11-05T10/abc123.png      (all writes this hour share a prefix)
✓ <tenant_id>/<user_id>/<uuid>.png      (writes spread across many prefixes)
```

AWS has greatly improved automatic partitioning, so you probably won't hit this at small scale, but doing it right from day one costs nothing.

### Rule 3 (the creator's preference): make the key carry ownership

With keys like `<tenant_id>/<user_id>/<object_id>`:

- an **authorization check** can be a simple **string comparison** in middleware ("does this key start with the current user's prefix?"), before you even contact S3,
- **access policies** can limit a set of credentials to exactly **one prefix**.

With flat random UUIDs, every authorization check needs a **database lookup**. One naming decision saves a network hop.

---

## 14. Inside object storage: data plane and metadata plane

What happens when you PUT a 100 MB object to S3?

1. The request lands on one of a huge fleet of **stateless front-end servers**.
2. That server **authenticates** it by **recomputing the request's signature** (section 20).
3. The work then splits into **two separate problems**, a core architectural idea of object storage:

| | **Data plane** | **Metadata plane** |
|---|---|---|
| Job | Store the bytes so they **survive** | Remember that key `uploads/2026/cat.png` in this bucket maps to **those pieces of data in those places** |
| Volume | **Huge** amounts of data | Small in comparison |
| Operations | Simple | **Enormous number** of operations |
| Requirements | Durability, low cost | Must be **strongly consistent** and **extremely fast** |

### Strong vs eventual consistency

- **Strongly consistent:** once a write succeeds, **every later read** sees it, even one a split second later.
- **Eventually consistent:** after a write there may be a **delay** before other readers see it; reads can briefly return old data or "not found".

The **metadata plane is the harder problem**. Storing exabytes on drives has been solved for decades. Keeping a **strongly consistent, globally distributed, sorted index** over hundreds of trillions of keys, with lookups in a few milliseconds, is extremely hard.

---

## 15. The data plane: replication vs erasure coding

### Naive: replication

Keep **three copies** on three machines in different **failure domains** (places that won't fail together). If one dies, copy from another.

- Simple and it works, but storing **1 PB** of customer data takes **3 PB** of drives: **200% overhead**. At cloud scale, that's billions of dollars.

### What large providers do: erasure coding

**Erasure coding** splits the data and adds mathematically computed redundancy:

1. Split an object into, say, **14 data shards**.
2. Run a mathematical transformation (the classic **Reed–Solomon** algorithm) that produces **6 parity shards**. That's **20 shards** in total.
3. Scatter the 20 shards over 20 drives in different racks, power domains and ideally buildings.
4. The key property: **any 14 of the 20 shards** are enough to rebuild the complete object. It doesn't matter which 14.

| | 3× replication | Erasure coding (14 + 6) |
|---|---|---|
| Storage used | 3× | 20 ÷ 14 ≈ **1.43×** |
| Failures tolerated | 2 lost copies | **6** lost shards |
| Extra cost | Lots of drives | **CPU** to compute parity, plus extra reads during recovery |

Erasure coding uses about half the storage **and** is more durable. CPU is cheap compared with drives, so the trade is very good.

*(14 + 6 is an example layout; providers don't publish exact parameters for every system.)*

---

## 16. Eleven nines, and why durability is not a backup

Amazon S3 is designed for **11 nines of durability: 99.999999999%** per object per year. Roughly: if you store **10 million objects**, you'd expect to lose **one** about **once every 10,000 years**. That figure comes from shard-placement maths like the above.

### Durability ≠ backup

Eleven nines protects you from **drives failing**. It does **not** protect you from **your own actions**:

- If a bug deletes everything under the wrong prefix, S3 will **durably, reliably and accurately** delete it all. You can't ask for it back.
- If a bug overwrites objects with corrupted data, S3 will faithfully keep the **corrupted** version.

If the data matters:

- **Turn on versioning.** Overwrites and deletes create a **new version** instead of destroying the old one.
- **Replicate to a second bucket in a different cloud account**, so that if one account's credentials are compromised, the attacker can't reach both.

---

## 17. The metadata plane: a giant sorted index

Conceptually, the metadata plane is a huge **sorted key–value index**, something like a **distributed B-tree** (a balanced tree also used by databases; see [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/12 Databases with Postgres/12 Databases with Postgres#16. Indexes|lesson 12]]). It maps **bucket + key** to the **locations of the shards** plus the size, ETag, content type and so on. The index is **partitioned by key range**, which is the cause of the hot-partition issue in section 13.

This structure explains several behaviours:

- **LIST is slow.** Listing (paginated at 1,000 keys) is a **range scan** over a distributed sorted index, much more expensive than a single key lookup.
- **No atomic rename.** Renaming changes the key, and the key decides which **partition** the entry lives in, so it isn't a simple in-place change.
- **Size and metadata are instant.** They come from the index, without touching any drive.

> [!important] Never put LIST in the request path
> **Your database should be the index** of which files exist. The bucket stores the bytes. Calling the list API on every request to answer "which files does this user have?" won't scale and adds latency.

### Consistency history

- Historically, S3 was **eventually consistent** for some operations. Upload an object, immediately GET it, and you might receive **404**, because the read hit an index replica that wasn't updated yet. Old blog posts and Stack Overflow answers recommend **retry loops or sleeps** after uploading because of this.
- Since **December 2020**, S3 provides **strong read-after-write consistency**: after a successful upload, an immediate read succeeds. Those workarounds are now **outdated**.

---

## 18. Conditional writes

For almost 20 years, a PUT **always overwrote** the existing object. If two processes wrote the same key at the same time, the last one silently won and the other's data was silently lost. There was **no way to detect it** and no way to say "write only if…". In other words, there was no **compare-and-swap** (CAS): an operation that updates a value only if it still equals what you expect.

In **2024**, S3 added **conditional writes**:

| Header | Meaning | If the condition fails |
|---|---|---|
| `If-None-Match: *` | Create the object **only if the key doesn't exist yet** | **412 Precondition Failed** |
| `If-Match: <etag>` | Replace the object **only if its current ETag is still the one I read** | **412 Precondition Failed** |

### Example: two clients updating the same object

1. Client A reads the object and gets ETag `E1`.
2. Client A edits it locally.
3. Meanwhile client B also writes the object, so S3 now has ETag `E2`.
4. Client A sends `PUT` with `If-Match: E1`. S3's current ETag is `E2`, so the write is **rejected with 412**.

Without the condition, A's write would have silently **overwritten B's**. With it, B's data is protected and A knows it must re-read and retry.

```bash
# Illustrative AWS CLI
aws s3api put-object --bucket demo-bucket --key lock.json --body lock.json --if-none-match '*'
# first time: 200 OK with an ETag
aws s3api put-object --bucket demo-bucket --key lock.json --body lock.json --if-none-match '*'
# second time: 412 Precondition Failed (the key already exists)
```

### Why this matters

Combined with strong consistency, conditional writes give object storage a **coordination primitive**: you can guarantee that **exactly one writer wins**. People now build **distributed locks**, **leader election** and even databases' **write-ahead logs** (an append-only log of changes that a database writes before applying them, which requires exactly one writer to win) on top of S3.

For everyday backends, the immediate benefit is simpler: an upload can **never silently overwrite an existing object**, which protects against the duplicate-key bug from section 13.

> [!warning] "S3-compatible" doesn't mean every feature
> Many providers are **S3-compatible**, meaning they speak the same API and work with the AWS SDKs (e.g. **Cloudflare R2**). Compatibility doesn't guarantee every feature, including conditional writes; Backblaze B2 was given as an example of one that lacked it. **Check the provider's documentation** before relying on it.

---

## 19. Upload architecture 1: through your server

How does a file get from a user's laptop into the bucket? The first option: **the browser sends the file to your API, and your backend forwards it to the bucket**.

**Pros:**

- Your backend sees **every byte**: it can validate the content, scan it, compute a hash and reject it before storing.
- Authorization is your normal **middleware**; no extra CORS setup.
- For **small files** (profile pictures, CSVs, documents of a few MB) it's acceptable, and it's used in practice.

### The hidden problem: buffering

Calling something like `ParseMultipartForm` in Go, or using a default body parser in a Node framework, reads the **whole file into RAM**. A 100 MB upload uses 100 MB of memory. **Twenty concurrent 100 MB uploads** use about **2 GB**, enough to hit the container's memory limit, get **OOM-killed** (out-of-memory) and restart. That's the disaster from section 2 again.

It doesn't show up in local development: you test with small files, on a fast network, on a machine with 16 GB+ of RAM.

### The fix: stream, and cap the size

**Stream** the body: read it in chunks and pass each chunk to the storage client as it arrives, so memory use stays roughly constant no matter how big the file is. Also **wrap the body in a size limit** before reading anything, so a 4 GB upload is cut off at your limit instead of being allowed to try.

```go
// Illustrative Go sketch (streaming upload to S3)
func uploadHandler(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
    r.Body = http.MaxBytesReader(w, r.Body, 50<<20) // hard cap: 50 MB

    mr, err := r.MultipartReader() // read parts one by one, no full parse
    if err != nil {
        http.Error(w, "bad request", http.StatusBadRequest)
        return
    }
    part, err := mr.NextPart()
    if err != nil {
        http.Error(w, "bad request", http.StatusBadRequest)
        return
    }

    key := newObjectKey(currentUserID(r)) // generated, never the user's file name
    _, err = uploader.Upload(r.Context(), &s3.PutObjectInput{
        Bucket: aws.String(bucket),
        Key:    aws.String(key),
        Body:   part, // the uploader reads from the stream chunk by chunk
    })
    ...
}
```

**Demo (shown in the lesson):** two servers each received the same 500 MB file while memory was watched with the `btop` monitor. The **buffered** server's memory climbed as the body arrived, ending about **500 MB higher**. The **streaming** server took the same time (about 6.5 s) but its memory line stayed **almost flat**.

### Limits streaming can't fix

Even with streaming, **bandwidth** becomes the bottleneck and the request stays open a long time:

- **Load balancers** often have an **idle timeout** of around **60 seconds** by default, which slow mobile uploads can hit.
- **Reverse proxies** like **NGINX** or **Caddy** have **body size limits**. NGINX is known for returning **413 Request Entity Too Large** exactly here.
- **Serverless functions and API gateways** have **hard payload limits** of a few megabytes that you **can't raise**.

So this architecture can work for small files on traditional servers, but it isn't the production-grade answer.

## 20. Upload architecture 2: pre-signed URLs

The production answer: **let the browser upload directly to the bucket**, so the bytes never pass through your server.

Two obstacles:

- The bucket must be **private**; public buckets are a major security risk.
- You can't give your storage **credentials** to the browser.

What's needed is a way to give the browser permission to do **exactly one operation**, on **exactly one key**, for **a few minutes**, without leaking credentials. That's a **pre-signed URL**.

### What a pre-signed URL contains

A normal URL with extra query parameters:

```text
https://my-bucket.s3.amazonaws.com/tenants/t_1/users/u_42/9f1c.png
  ?X-Amz-Algorithm=AWS4-HMAC-SHA256
  &X-Amz-Credential=AKIA…/20261105/us-east-1/s3/aws4_request
  &X-Amz-Date=20261105T120000Z
  &X-Amz-Expires=60
  &X-Amz-SignedHeaders=host
  &X-Amz-Signature=3f9c…
```

*(Illustrative values.)*

- the signing **algorithm**,
- your **access key ID** (which identifies the key, but isn't secret),
- a **timestamp** and an **expiry** in seconds,
- which **headers** are covered by the signature,
- the **signature**: an **HMAC** (a keyed hash) computed over a string describing the request (HTTP method, bucket, key, expiry…) using your **secret key**.

### How it's verified

1. Your **server** generates the URL using the secret key, which never leaves the server.
2. The **browser** sends a `PUT` to that URL.
3. **S3** rebuilds the same string from the incoming request, computes the HMAC with **its own copy of the secret**, and compares.
4. If they match and the URL hasn't expired, the request is allowed. If the browser changes **even one character** of the key or method, or uses the URL **after expiry**, the signatures don't match and the request is **rejected (403)**.

The credential never leaves your server, but the browser gets a narrow, temporary **capability**.

**Demo (shown in the lesson):**

- the page asked its own server for a signed URL, which came back with a **60-second** expiry,
- the browser's network panel showed a `PUT` going **straight to the bucket's domain**, carrying no credentials, and S3 returned **200**,
- resending the same request after 60 seconds gave **403 Forbidden**,
- changing one character of the key while the URL was still valid also gave **403** (signature mismatch).

## 21. Limiting uploads with a pre-signed POST policy

There's a hole: a pre-signed **PUT** URL issued "for a profile picture" signs the method, bucket and key, but **nothing limits the body size**. A user could upload a **5 GB** file to it.

The fix is a **pre-signed POST** with a **policy**. Instead of signing a URL, your server signs a small **JSON policy document** and gives the client a **URL plus a set of form fields**. The policy contains **conditions** that **the storage service itself enforces**:

```json
{
  "expiration": "2026-11-05T12:05:00Z",
  "conditions": [
    { "bucket": "my-app-uploads" },
    ["starts-with", "$key", "tenants/t_1/users/u_42/"],
    ["starts-with", "$Content-Type", "image/"],
    ["content-length-range", 1024, 5242880]
  ]
}
```

*(Illustrative policy.)*

- **`content-length-range`**: a hard minimum and maximum size (here 1 KB to 5 MB), enforced by S3 without your server.
- **Content type** must start with `image/`.
- **Key** must start with this tenant's and user's prefix, so the client can't write outside its own "folder".

If any condition fails, S3 **rejects the request and stores nothing**.

On the client:

```js
// Illustrative browser code
const form = new FormData();
for (const [name, value] of Object.entries(fields)) form.append(name, value);
form.append("file", file); // the file field must come LAST

await fetch(url, { method: "POST", body: form });
// don't set Content-Type yourself: the browser must add the multipart boundary
```

**Demo (shown in the lesson):**

- **without a policy**, a 300 MB file uploaded to a URL meant for a profile picture was accepted with **200**, leaving about **314 million bytes** in the bucket,
- **with a policy**, the same file was rejected with **400 EntityTooLarge** and nothing was stored,
- a **415 KB** image with the same policy **succeeded**,
- trying to write under **another user's prefix** was refused with **403**, and S3 named the failed condition.

## 22. The two-phase upload flow and cleanup

If the browser uploads directly to storage, **your server never sees the upload**. How does the database learn about the file, so later requests can find it? With a **two-phase flow**:

```text
Phase 1  Browser ──"I want to upload"──▶ Backend
                                         • authorize the user
                                         • generate the object key
                                         • INSERT row (status = 'pending', key, limits…)
         Browser ◀── pre-signed POST URL + fields + upload ID ──

         Browser ════ file bytes ════▶ Bucket   (server not involved)

Phase 2  Browser ──"done", upload ID──▶ Backend
                                         • HEAD the object in the bucket
                                         • exists? size and content type as expected?
                                         • UPDATE row SET status = 'ready'
```

- In phase 1, the database records the **intent** and the object's identity **before any bytes move**.
- The completion call sends the **upload ID**, not the key.
- **HEAD** fetches only an object's metadata, not its bytes, so it's very cheap. It confirms the object exists with the expected size and type.

### Cleanup: abandoned uploads

Some uploads will never complete: connections drop, tabs close, mobile networks fail, or the file arrives but the completion call never happens. So you need a cleanup path:

- a **lifecycle rule** on the bucket that automatically deletes objects under a pending prefix after **24 hours**, and
- a small **background job** (see [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/14 Task Queues and Background Jobs/14 Task Queues and Background Jobs|lesson 14]]) that finds rows still `pending` after 24 hours and marks them **expired**.

This keeps the two **sources of truth** from drifting apart:

- the **database** is the source of truth for **which files exist**,
- the **bucket** is the source of truth for **the bytes**.

Whenever they disagree, a background process must reconcile them. This is the practical answer to problem 6 (section 8).

## 23. CORS for direct uploads

When the browser uploads directly to S3, Cloudflare R2, Backblaze B2 or similar, it's sending a request to a **different origin** from your frontend, so **CORS** applies (see [[Notes/Backend from First Principles/05 HTTP for Backend Engineers/05 HTTP for Backend Engineers#7. CORS and the OPTIONS method|lesson 05]]). The **bucket's CORS configuration** must:

- **allow your frontend's origin**,
- **allow the PUT or POST method**,
- **expose the `ETag` header** (needed for multipart uploads in part 2).

```json
[
  {
    "AllowedOrigins": ["https://app.example.com"],
    "AllowedMethods": ["PUT", "POST"],
    "AllowedHeaders": ["*"],
    "ExposeHeaders": ["ETag"],
    "MaxAgeSeconds": 3000
  }
]
```

*(Illustrative S3 CORS configuration.)*

> [!tip] Debugging hint
> If an upload works with **curl** or **Postman** but fails in the **browser**, check the bucket's **CORS** settings first. Those tools don't enforce CORS; browsers do.

## Key takeaways

- Saving uploads on the server's disk fails in production: **ephemeral containers**, **multiple instances**, **fixed-size disks**, **single-copy durability**, **slow downloads tying up servers**, and **no transaction** between files and DB rows.
- Storage comes in three kinds: **block** (fast, primitive, one machine), **file** (rich POSIX interface, hard to scale), and **object** (minimal interface, near-infinite scale).
- Object storage offers **PUT, GET, DELETE, LIST** only: objects are **immutable**, there's no rename, and **folders are just key prefixes**.
- **Generate keys yourself**, put randomness early, and consider encoding ownership (`tenant/user/object`).
- Internally: a **data plane** (erasure coding gives about 1.43× overhead with better durability than 3× replication) and a **strongly consistent metadata plane** (a distributed sorted index).
- **Eleven nines of durability is not a backup.** Use versioning and cross-account replication.
- **Your database is the index of files**; don't LIST in the request path.
- **Conditional writes** (`If-None-Match`, `If-Match` → 412) give object storage compare-and-swap.
- If uploads go through your server, **stream** and **cap the size**. Better: **pre-signed URLs**, with **POST policies** to enforce size, type and prefix.
- Use a **two-phase flow** (pending row → direct upload → HEAD check → ready) plus **cleanup**, and configure **CORS** on the bucket.

- **Clarifications:**
  - ext4 and NTFS are **file systems**, not block storage; they're built on top of block devices. The note puts them under file storage.
  - Databases like PostgreSQL normally run on a file system that sits on block storage, rather than bypassing the file system. The note just says they run on block storage for speed.
  - Some block volumes (e.g. EBS Multi-Attach) can attach to more than one machine; the "one machine at a time" rule is the normal case.
  - The editor example is described in the transcript as copying to a new file and deleting the old ones. The usual technique is write-to-temp-then-rename, which is what the note describes.
  - The transcript says "any one part out of those 14" can rebuild the object; it means **any 14 of the 20** shards.
  - Bucket **names** must be globally unique; keys only need to be unique within a bucket.
  - HEAD requests are billed (cheaply) on S3, not free.
  - The transcript says I/O-bound work should be avoided. The note keeps the point that serving file bytes is work the app server shouldn't need to do, since lesson 22 treats I/O-bound work as normal and handled with concurrency.
  - S3 added `If-None-Match` in August 2024 and `If-Match` in November 2024; the note says "2024". Provider support changes over time, so check current docs (including Backblaze B2's).
  - The AWS SDK's upload manager streams the body but buffers one part at a time (several MB by default), not just a few kilobytes.
  - A lifecycle rule deleting a "pending prefix" assumes pending uploads use a separate prefix or tag; completed objects must not live under it.
